claim: HCMV infection increases 45S pre-rRNA levels as early as three hours post-infection.
source: Figure 1A shows that increased 45S rRNA levels were detected in HCMV-infected compared to mock-infected cells as early as three hpi.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A comparing mock-infected and HCMV-infected cells at multiple time points.

claim: 45S rRNA levels in HCMV-infected cells reach approximately 6-fold greater than mock-infected cells at 24 hours post-infection.
source: This continued to increase, reaching its zenith at 24 hpi where 45S rRNA levels were approximately 6-fold greater in HCMV-infected cells than mock-infected cells.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Nucleolar size increases in HCMV-infected cells.
source: Consistent with increased 45S rRNA accumulation, immunostaining for fibrillarin, a component marking fibrillar centers of nucleoli (Németh and Grummt, 2018) revealed that nucleolar size increased in HCMV-infected cells and that nucleolar integrity appeared intact (Figure 1B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging of fibrillarin in Figure 1B and citation to established nucleolar marker.

claim: HCMV infection stimulates FU incorporation in discrete sub-nuclear foci resembling nucleoli.
source: Figure 1C demonstrates that FU incorporation was stimulated and areas of FU staining were enlarged in response to HCMV infection. Under these conditions, the majority of FU staining was confined within discrete sub-nuclear foci in uninfected or HCMV-infected cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Metabolic labeling with 5-Fluoruridine followed by immunofluorescence detection shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HCMV infection stimulates RNAPI reporter activity at 24 hours post-infection.
source: In response to HCMV infection, a significant increase in RNAPI reporter activity was detected at 24 hpi (Figure 1D), demonstrating that HCMV stimulates transcription from cellular RNAPI-specific promoters.
evidence: Reporter assay data using pHrP2-BH plasmid shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The abundance of RNAPI transcription factors TIF-IA and UBF increases by six hours post-infection with HCMV.
source: Compared to mock-infected cells, the abundance of the RNAPI transcription factors TIF-IA and UBF increased by six hpi coincident with detection of UL44, a representative early viral protein (Figure 1E).
evidence: Immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1E demonstrating increased protein levels.

claim: TIF-IA and UBF protein levels reach peak levels by 48 hours post-infection and remain elevated at 72 hours post-infection.
source: TIF-IA and UBF reached peak levels by 48hpi, and remained elevated even at 72hpi (Figure 1E).
evidence: Time course immunoblotting data in Figure 1E.

claim: TIF-IA siRNA effectively reduces 45S pre-rRNA steady-state levels in HCMV infected cells.
source: Compared to non-silencing siRNA, both TIF-IA siRNAs effectively reduced 45S pre-rRNA steady-state levels in HCMV infected cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: RT-qPCR data comparing control and TIF-IA siRNA treated cells shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TIF-IA depletion causes a substantial decrease in 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits and 80S monoribosomes in HCMV-infected cells.
source: Sucrose gradient fractionation of cytoplasmic lysates from HCMV-infected cells revealed a substantial decrease in 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits and 80S monoribosomes in cells treated with TIF-IA specific siRNA compared to control siRNA (Figure 2B).
evidence: Polysome profiling data shown in Figure 2B comparing control and TIF-IA siRNA.

claim: TIF-IA depletion has a modest impact on actively translating polyribosomes in HCMV-infected cells.
source: However, a more modest impact on actively translating polyribosomes was observed, indicating that polysome assembly proceeds in HCMV-infected cells even when ribosome biogenesis is restricted (Figure 2B).
evidence: Polysome profiling data in Figure 2B showing polysome region.

claim: TIF-IA depletion impairs global protein synthesis in uninfected cells.
source: Unexpectedly, while TIF-IA depletion impaired global protein synthesis in uninfected cells (Figure 2C,E), it had no detectable impact in HCMV-infected cells (Figure 2D,F).
evidence: 35S-amino acid labeling data shown in Figures 2C and 2E.

claim: TIF-IA depletion has no detectable impact on global protein synthesis in HCMV-infected cells.
source: Unexpectedly, while TIF-IA depletion impaired global protein synthesis in uninfected cells (Figure 2C,E), it had no detectable impact in HCMV-infected cells (Figure 2D,F).
evidence: 35S-amino acid labeling data shown in Figures 2D and 2F.

claim: TIF-IA depletion enhances HCMV virus reproduction and dissemination.
source: Compared with control siRNA-treated cultures, a greater number of eGFP-positive cells were detected in TIF-IA-depleted cultures (Figure 3B), indicating that TIF-IA depletion enhanced virus reproduction and dissemination.
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy data showing increased eGFP-positive cells in Figure 3B.

claim: TIF-IA depletion substantially increases the abundance of representative early (UL44) and late (pp28) viral proteins.
source: Immunoblotting of cellular lysates revealed that the abundance of representative early (UL44), and late (pp28) viral proteins all increased substantially upon TIF-IA depletion (Figure 3C).
evidence: Immunoblotting data in Figure 3C showing increased viral protein levels.

claim: TIF-IA depletion enhances infectious virus production by up to 100-fold.
source: Furthermore, TIF-IA depletion enhanced infectious virus production by up to 100-fold (Figure 3D).
evidence: TCID50 assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: UBF depletion results in greater numbers of eGFP-positive cells, more viral protein accumulation, and greater amounts of infectious virus in HCMV-infected cultures.
source: Similar to results obtained following TIF-IA depletion, greater numbers of eGFP-positive cells, more viral protein accumulation, and greater amounts of infectious virus were produced in HCMV-infected cultures upon UBF-depletion (Figure 3E,F,G).
evidence: Data from Figures 3E, 3F, and 3G showing effects of UBF depletion.

claim: TFIIIA depletion results in greater numbers of eGFP-positive cells, higher levels of viral proteins, and increased infectious virus production.
source: Furthermore, greater numbers of eGFP-positive cells, higher levels of representative viral proteins and increased infectious virus production were observed in cultures treated with TFIIIA or BOP1-siRNAs compared to non-silencing, control siRNA (Figure 3H–M).
evidence: Data from Figures 3H-3M showing effects of TFIIIA depletion.

claim: BOP1 depletion results in greater numbers of eGFP-positive cells, higher levels of viral proteins, and increased infectious virus production.
source: Furthermore, greater numbers of eGFP-positive cells, higher levels of representative viral proteins and increased infectious virus production were observed in cultures treated with TFIIIA or BOP1-siRNAs compared to non-silencing, control siRNA (Figure 3H–M).
evidence: Data from Figures 3H-3M showing effects of BOP1 depletion.

claim: Depleting TIF-IA, UBF, TFIIIA, or BOP1 reduces levels of representative ISG-encoded mRNAs in HCMV-infected primary fibroblasts.
source: Compared to HCMV-infected cultures treated with non-silencing siRNA, reduced levels of representative ISG-encoded mRNAs (Figure 4A) and proteins (Figure 4B) accumulated in cultures depleted for either of the RNAPI transcription factors TIF-IA or UBF, the 5S RNA RNAPIII transcription factor TFIIIA, or the rRNA processing factor BOP1.
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 4A showing reduced ISG mRNA levels.

claim: Depleting TIF-IA, UBF, TFIIIA, or BOP1 reduces levels of representative ISG-encoded proteins in HCMV-infected primary fibroblasts.
source: Compared to HCMV-infected cultures treated with non-silencing siRNA, reduced levels of representative ISG-encoded mRNAs (Figure 4A) and proteins (Figure 4B) accumulated in cultures depleted for either of the RNAPI transcription factors TIF-IA or UBF, the 5S RNA RNAPIII transcription factor TFIIIA, or the rRNA processing factor BOP1.
evidence: Immunoblotting data in Figure 4B showing reduced ISG protein levels.

claim: JAK inhibitor treatment equalizes viral protein levels between non-silencing siRNA and ribosome biogenesis inhibition siRNA-treated cells.
source: In contrast to DMSO-treated cells where viral protein abundance was far less in cells exposed to non-silencing siRNA compared to siRNAs that inhibited ribosome biogenesis, viral protein levels in JAKi-treated cells exposed to non-silencing siRNA were approximately equivalent to those detected in TIF-IA, UBF, TFIIIA, or BOP1 siRNA-treated NHDFs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Immunoblotting data in Figure 4C comparing DMSO and JAKi treatment conditions.

claim: TIF-IA depletion significantly reduces IFNB1 mRNA accumulation in response to HCMV infection at six hours post-infection.
source: Surprisingly, accumulation of IFNB1 mRNA and a representative ISG-encoded polypeptide (IFIT2 protein) were significantly reduced in response to HCMV infection when cells were treated with TIF-IA siRNA compared to non-silencing siRNA (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 4D showing reduced IFNB1 mRNA levels.

claim: TIF-IA depletion reduces IFIT2 protein accumulation in response to HCMV infection at 48 hours post-infection.
source: Surprisingly, accumulation of IFNB1 mRNA and a representative ISG-encoded polypeptide (IFIT2 protein) were significantly reduced in response to HCMV infection when cells were treated with TIF-IA siRNA compared to non-silencing siRNA (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Immunoblotting data in Figure 4E showing reduced IFIT2 protein levels.

claim: TIF-IA depletion has no detectable impact on IFNB1 mRNA accumulation in response to VSV infection.
source: As depleting TIF-IA had no detectable impact on IFNB1 mRNA accumulation in response to infection with the RNA virus vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), this suggested that rRNA biogenesis selectively influenced IFNB1 induction in response to viruses like HCMV with dsDNA genomes (Figure 4F) (Yanai et al., 2009).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 4F comparing IFNB1 response to VSV infection.

claim: UV-inactivated HCMV stimulates 45S rRNA accumulation.
source: Figure 5A shows that UV-inactivated HCMV stimulated 45S rRNA accumulation, which suggested that viral gene expression was not required to induce rRNA accumulation and is consistent with rRNA accumulation being triggered in response to either a virion protein component or a pathogen- associated molecular pattern like a nucleic acid.
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 5A comparing mock-infected and UV-inactivated HCMV infected cells.

claim: 45S rRNA abundance increases following treatment with two different immunostimulatory synthetic dsDNAs.
source: Indeed, 45S rRNA abundance increased following treatment with two different immunostimulatory synthetic dsDNAs, but not the same single-stranded DNA sequences (Figure 5B).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 5B showing response to different DNA types.

claim: 45S rRNA abundance does not increase following treatment with single-stranded DNA sequences.
source: Indeed, 45S rRNA abundance increased following treatment with two different immunostimulatory synthetic dsDNAs, but not the same single-stranded DNA sequences (Figure 5B).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 5B showing lack of response to single-stranded DNA.

claim: Circular plasmid dsDNA from bacteria stimulates 45S rRNA accumulation.
source: Similarly, circular plasmid dsDNA from bacteria stimulated 45S rRNA accumulation (Figure 5B).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 5B showing response to plasmid DNA.

claim: TIF-IA depletion reduces IFNB1 mRNA accumulation in response to synthetic immunostimulatory dsDNA in uninfected cells.
source: Compared with non-silencing siRNA-treated cells, accumulation of IFNB1 mRNA and two representative ISG-encoded proteins, USP18 and IFIT2, was reduced in TIF-IA-depleted cells exposed to dsDNA (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 5C showing reduced IFNB1 mRNA in TIF-IA depleted cells.

claim: TIF-IA depletion reduces USP18 and IFIT2 protein accumulation in response to synthetic immunostimulatory dsDNA in uninfected cells.
source: Compared with non-silencing siRNA-treated cells, accumulation of IFNB1 mRNA and two representative ISG-encoded proteins, USP18 and IFIT2, was reduced in TIF-IA-depleted cells exposed to dsDNA (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Immunoblotting data in Figure 5D showing reduced ISG protein levels.

claim: UBF depletion reduces IFNB1 mRNA accumulation in response to synthetic immunostimulatory dsDNA in uninfected cells.
source: Cells treated with ns siRNA, TIF-IA siRNA, or UBF siRNA were transfected with dsDNA. Similar to observations in TIF-IA depleted cells, IFNB1 mRNA accumulated to reduced levels in cells treated with UBF siRNA compared with non-silencing siRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Induction of all genes most highly-induced (>4 fold) by dsDNA is reduced by depleting either TIF-IA or UBF.
source: Strikingly, induction of all the genes most highly-induced (>4 fold) by dsDNA was reduced by depleting either TIF-IA or UBF (Figure 5E; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E heatmap.

claim: TIF-IA depletion results in 1392 genes being downregulated and 1743 genes being upregulated.
source: Following normalization and classification of differentially regulated genes (adjusted P-value [Padj] of <0.01), 3135 genes proved responsive to TIF-IA depletion compared to non-silencing siRNA control-treated cultures. While 1392 genes were downregulated following TIF-IA- depletion, 1743 genes were upregulated (Figure 6A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6A volcano plot.

claim: Genes in pathways controlling mitotic nuclear division are downregulated in TIF-IA depleted cells compared to control.
source: Gene ontology analysis showed that compared to non-silencing (ns) control siRNA treated cells, genes in pathways controlling mitotic nuclear division (p<3.90E-23), cell division (p<9.12E-19), sister chromatid cohesion (p<2.07E-13), cell proliferation (p<6.60E-07), regulation of cell cycle (p<2.42E-05) and G2/M transition of mitotic cell cycle (p<5.76E-04) were down regulated in TIF-IA depleted cells (Figure 6B), consistent with the role for ribosome biogenesis in cellular growth and proliferation (Donati et al., 2012).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis results shown in Figure 6B with statistical significance values.

claim: Expression of genes responsive to the transcription factor Nuclear Factor-Y (NF-Y) are selectively repressed by TIF-IA depletion.
source: Results of this analysis revealed that expression of genes responsive to the transcription factor Nuclear Factor-Y (NF-Y) were found to be selectively repressed by TIF-IA-depletion (Figure 6C).
evidence: TRANSFAC analysis results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: NF-Y target genes overlap significantly (p=2.2×10−16) with DREAM complex targets.
source: Furthermore, NF-Y target genes reportedly overlap significantly (p=2.2×10−16) with DREAM complex targets (Sadasivam et al., 2012), and many DREAM target genes encode cell cycle genes indirectly repressed by p53 (Fischer et al., 2016).
evidence: Statistical overlap value cited from published literature.

claim: p53 accumulates in response to TIF-IA depletion.
source: Indeed, p53 accumulated in response to TIF-IA depletion (Figure 6D) in agreement with published studies (Yuan et al., 2005) and consistent with our observed changes in p53 target gene expression.
evidence: Immunoblotting data in Figure 6D and citation to prior work.

claim: TIF-IA depletion decreases levels of five different DREAM target genes: HMGB2, CENPF, CDK1, TK1, and CDCA8.
source: Measuring gene expression by qPCR following TIF-IA depletion demonstrated that levels for five different DREAM target genes [HMGB2, CENPF, CDK1, TK1, and CDCA8] decreased, effectively validating the results of our genome-wide analysis (Figure 6E).
evidence: RT-qPCR validation data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The reduction of HMGB2 mRNA in response to TIF-IA depletion is p53-dependent.
source: Moreover, the reduction of HMGB2 mRNA in response to TIF-IA depletion was p53-dependent as measured by qRT-PCR (Figure 6F), in accord with prior genome-wide data (Fischer et al., 2016).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 6F showing p53 dependence and citation to prior work.

claim: HMGB2 abundance is reduced in TIF-IA siRNA-treated cells compared to non-silencing siRNA-treated cells.
source: Compared to NHDFs treated with non-silencing siRNA, HMGB2 abundance was reduced in TIF-IA siRNA-treated cells whereas actin levels remained relatively constant. (Figure 7A).
evidence: Immunoblotting data in Figure 7A showing reduced HMGB2 protein levels.

claim: RNA pol I selective inhibitor CX-5461 reduces HMGB2 mRNA and protein levels.
source: A similar reduction in HMGB2 mRNA and protein levels was observed in NHDFs treated with the RNA pol I selective inhibitor CX-5461 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: RT-qPCR and immunoblotting data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reduction in HMGB2 mRNA abundance in response to CX-5461 is dependent upon p53.
source: In addition, the reduction in HMGB2 mRNA abundance in response to CX-5461 was dependent upon p53 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 showing p53 dependence.

claim: TIF-IA depletion selectively reduces HMGB2 protein abundance in the cytoplasm while nuclear HMGB2 remains detectable.
source: In NHDFs treated with non-silencing siRNA, HMGB2 was detected throughout the cell in both cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments. However, although nuclear HMGB2 was readily detected in TIF-IA depleted NHDFs, cytoplasmic HMGB2 staining was unexpectedly lost (Figure 7B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data in Figure 7B showing subcellular localization.

claim: HMGB2 depletion significantly reduces IFNB1 mRNA accumulation in response to HCMV infection.
source: Compared to non-silencing (ns) control siRNA treated cultures, significantly less IFNB1 mRNA accumulated in response to HCMV infection upon HMGB2-depletion (Figure 7C).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 7C showing reduced IFNB1 mRNA.

claim: HMGB2 depletion has no detectable impact on IFNB1 accumulation induced in response to VSV infection.
source: By contrast, HMGB2-depletion had no detectable impact on IFNB1 accumulation induced in response to infection with VSV, an RNA virus (Figure 7D), in agreement with reports showing HMGB2 was dispensable for IFNB1 induction by RNA in murine cells (Yanai et al., 2009).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 7D and citation to prior work in murine cells.

claim: HMGB2 depletion does not detectably reduce IFNB1 mRNA accumulation in response to cGAMP treatment.
source: Compared to ns siRNA-treated cultures, IFNB1 mRNA accumulation in response to cGAMP was not detectably reduced by HMGB2-depletion (Figure 7E).
evidence: RT-qPCR data in Figure 7E showing response to cGAMP.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis is among the most energetically demanding processes in the cell.
source: It is among the most energetically demanding processes in the cell and requires all three eukaryotic RNA polymerases.
evidence: Statement based on established biological knowledge about cellular energetics.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis requires all three eukaryotic RNA polymerases.
source: It is among the most energetically demanding processes in the cell and requires all three eukaryotic RNA polymerases.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of ribosome biogenesis machinery.

claim: The 47S precursor-rRNA (pre-rRNA) is transcribed by RNA Polymerase I (RNAPI) within the nucleolus.
source: While the 47S precursor-rRNA (pre-rRNA) is transcribed by RNA Polymerase I (RNAPI) within the nucleolus, 5S rRNA is generated by RNA Polymerase III (RNAPIII) and mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins are produced by RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII) in the nucleoplasm.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of ribosome biogenesis.

claim: 5S rRNA is generated by RNA Polymerase III (RNAPIII).
source: While the 47S precursor-rRNA (pre-rRNA) is transcribed by RNA Polymerase I (RNAPI) within the nucleolus, 5S rRNA is generated by RNA Polymerase III (RNAPIII) and mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins are produced by RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII) in the nucleoplasm.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of ribosome biogenesis.

claim: mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins are produced by RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII) in the nucleoplasm.
source: While the 47S precursor-rRNA (pre-rRNA) is transcribed by RNA Polymerase I (RNAPI) within the nucleolus, 5S rRNA is generated by RNA Polymerase III (RNAPIII) and mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins are produced by RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII) in the nucleoplasm.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of ribosome biogenesis.

claim: 47S pre-rRNA is processed into mature 5.8S, 18S, and 28S rRNA.
source: Following processing of 47S pre-rRNA into mature 5.8S, 18S, and 28S rRNA, assembly of large 60S and small 40S ribosomal subunits from rRNA and ribosomal protein components commences in the nucleolus (Mayer and Grummt, 2006).
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge with citation to prior work.

claim: Assembly of large 60S and small 40S ribosomal subunits commences in the nucleolus.
source: Following processing of 47S pre-rRNA into mature 5.8S, 18S, and 28S rRNA, assembly of large 60S and small 40S ribosomal subunits from rRNA and ribosomal protein components commences in the nucleolus (Mayer and Grummt, 2006).
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge with citation to prior work.

claim: Dysregulation of ribosome biogenesis contributes to cancer.
source: While ribosome biogenesis is fundamental for normal cell growth, development and differentiation, its dysregulation contributes to diverse diseases including cancer, where it is stimulated, and genetic disorders collectively termed ribosomopathies where it is often impaired (Aspesi and Ellis, 2019; Mills and Green, 2017; Narla and Ebert, 2010; Pelletier et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis is stimulated in cancer.
source: While ribosome biogenesis is fundamental for normal cell growth, development and differentiation, its dysregulation contributes to diverse diseases including cancer, where it is stimulated, and genetic disorders collectively termed ribosomopathies where it is often impaired (Aspesi and Ellis, 2019; Mills and Green, 2017; Narla and Ebert, 2010; Pelletier et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis is often impaired in genetic disorders collectively termed ribosomopathies.
source: While ribosome biogenesis is fundamental for normal cell growth, development and differentiation, its dysregulation contributes to diverse diseases including cancer, where it is stimulated, and genetic disorders collectively termed ribosomopathies where it is often impaired (Aspesi and Ellis, 2019; Mills and Green, 2017; Narla and Ebert, 2010; Pelletier et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Interfering with ribosome biogenesis triggers a nucleolar stress response whereby p53 is stabilized and the cell cycle is blocked.
source: Interfering with ribosome biogenesis triggers a nucleolar stress response whereby p53 is stabilized and the cell cycle is blocked (Boulon et al., 2010; Chakraborty et al., 2011; Deisenroth et al., 2016; Golomb et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Several viruses reportedly stimulated rRNA synthesis upon infection.
source: Indeed, several viruses reportedly stimulated rRNA synthesis upon infection (May et al., 1976; Pöckl and Wintersberger, 1980; Soprano et al., 1983).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Host protein synthesis proceeds in cells infected with Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV).
source: In contrast to viruses that shut off host mRNA translation, host protein synthesis proceeds in cells infected with Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV) (Walsh et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HCMV upregulates the translation of mRNAs encoding functions involved in ribosome biogenesis.
source: Moreover, HCMV upregulates the translation of mRNAs encoding functions involved in ribosome biogenesis and increases the steady state levels of ribosomes (McKinney et al., 2014; Tirosh et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HCMV increases the steady state levels of ribosomes.
source: Moreover, HCMV upregulates the translation of mRNAs encoding functions involved in ribosome biogenesis and increases the steady state levels of ribosomes (McKinney et al., 2014; Tirosh et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HMGB2-deficient murine cells are defective for type I interferon and inflammatory cytokine induction in response to dsDNA.
source: HMGB2 figured prominently among this set of genes as HMGB2-deficient murine cells have been previously shown to be defective for type I interferon and inflammatory cytokine induction in response to dsDNA and HMGB2 has been proposed to play a critical role in cytoplasmic dsDNA signaling (Lee et al., 2013; Yanai et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature in murine cells.

claim: HMGB2 has been proposed to play a critical role in cytoplasmic dsDNA signaling.
source: HMGB2 figured prominently among this set of genes as HMGB2-deficient murine cells have been previously shown to be defective for type I interferon and inflammatory cytokine induction in response to dsDNA and HMGB2 has been proposed to play a critical role in cytoplasmic dsDNA signaling (Lee et al., 2013; Yanai et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HMGB2 is a non-specific dsDNA binding protein that is loosely associated with chromatin.
source: HMGB2 is a non-specific dsDNA binding protein that is loosely associated with chromatin (Malarkey and Churchill, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: HMGB proteins are alarmins that upon release from injured cells are capable of activating immune cells and evoking inflammation.
source: In addition, HMGB proteins are alarmins and upon release from injured cells are capable of activating immune cells and evoking inflammation (Harris et al., 2012; Yanai et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nuclear retention of HMGB family members limits inflammation.
source: Nuclear retention of HMGB family members limits inflammation (Avgousti et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: HMGB2 facilitates sensing of long dsDNA by cGAS.
source: HMGB2 facilitates sensing of long dsDNA by cGAS (Andreeva et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Both cGAS and HMGB2 regulate senescence.
source: In addition to IFNB1 production, both cGAS and HMGB2 regulate senescence and HMGB2 plays a role controlling the senescence-associated secretory pathway (Aird et al., 2016; Guerrero and Gil, 2016; Yang et al., 2017; Zirkel et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HMGB2 plays a role controlling the senescence-associated secretory pathway.
source: In addition to IFNB1 production, both cGAS and HMGB2 regulate senescence and HMGB2 plays a role controlling the senescence-associated secretory pathway (Aird et al., 2016; Guerrero and Gil, 2016; Yang et al., 2017; Zirkel et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Restricting ribosome biogenesis stimulated HCMV replication without suppressing translation.
source: Surprisingly, we find that restricting ribosome biogenesis stimulated human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) replication without suppressing translation.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract based on experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Interfering with ribosomal RNA (rRNA) accumulation triggered nucleolar stress and repressed expression of 1392 genes.
source: Interfering with ribosomal RNA (rRNA) accumulation triggered nucleolar stress and repressed expression of 1392 genes, including High Mobility Group Box 2 (HMGB2), a chromatin-associated protein that facilitates cytoplasmic double-stranded (ds) DNA-sensing by cGAS.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract based on RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Restricting ribosome biogenesis reduced cytoplasmic HMGB2 abundance.
source: Furthermore, it reduced cytoplasmic HMGB2 abundance and impaired induction of interferon beta (IFNB1) mRNA, which encodes a critical anti-proliferative, proinflammatory cytokine, in response to HCMV or dsDNA in uninfected cells.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract based on immunofluorescence data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Restricting ribosome biogenesis impaired induction of interferon beta (IFNB1) mRNA in response to HCMV.
source: Furthermore, it reduced cytoplasmic HMGB2 abundance and impaired induction of interferon beta (IFNB1) mRNA, which encodes a critical anti-proliferative, proinflammatory cytokine, in response to HCMV or dsDNA in uninfected cells.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract based on RT-qPCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Restricting ribosome biogenesis impaired induction of interferon beta (IFNB1) mRNA in response to dsDNA in uninfected cells.
source: Furthermore, it reduced cytoplasmic HMGB2 abundance and impaired induction of interferon beta (IFNB1) mRNA, which encodes a critical anti-proliferative, proinflammatory cytokine, in response to HCMV or dsDNA in uninfected cells.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract based on RT-qPCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: rRNA accumulation regulates innate immune responses to dsDNA by controlling HMGB2 abundance.
source: This establishes that rRNA accumulation regulates innate immune responses to dsDNA by controlling HMGB2 abundance.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings including HMGB2 depletion and TIF-IA depletion experiments.

claim: rRNA accumulation and/or nucleolar activity regulate dsDNA-sensing to restrict virus reproduction and regulate inflammation.
source: Moreover, it reveals that rRNA accumulation and/or nucleolar activity unexpectedly regulate dsDNA-sensing to restrict virus reproduction and regulate inflammation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings showing effects on virus replication and IFNB1 induction.

claim: The HCMV-induced increase in ribosome abundance is dispensable for efficient protein synthesis during infection.
source: This indicated that the HCMV-induced increase in ribosome abundance, which was presumed important for the infected cell protein synthesis program, is dispensable for efficient protein synthesis during infection and that ribosome abundance per se was not limiting infected cell protein synthesis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from 35S-amino acid labeling experiments showing no impact of TIF-IA depletion on protein synthesis in infected cells.

claim: Ribosome abundance per se is not limiting infected cell protein synthesis in HCMV-infected cells.
source: This indicated that the HCMV-induced increase in ribosome abundance, which was presumed important for the infected cell protein synthesis program, is dispensable for efficient protein synthesis during infection and that ribosome abundance per se was not limiting infected cell protein synthesis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from 35S-amino acid labeling experiments showing no impact of TIF-IA depletion on protein synthesis in infected cells.

claim: HCMV replication is restricted by the host RNAPI transcription factor TIF-IA.
source: These results establish that HCMV replication is restricted by the host RNAPI transcription factor TIF-IA.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing enhanced virus replication upon TIF-IA depletion.

claim: Interfering with ribosome biogenesis by depleting TIF-IA, UBF, TFIIIA or BOP1 limits JAK-dependent signaling perhaps by modulating type I interferon production.
source: In addition, it is consistent with the notion that ribosome biogenesis in HCMV-infected cells is required to establish an anti-viral state dependent upon ISG expression that limits virus replication. Finally, it further suggests that inhibiting ribosome biogenesis by interfering with TIF-IA, UBF, TFIIIA or BOP1 limited JAK-dependent signaling perhaps by modulating type I interferon production.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from JAK inhibitor experiments showing equalization of viral protein levels.

claim: rRNA biogenesis selectively influences IFNB1 induction in response to viruses with dsDNA genomes.
source: As depleting TIF-IA had no detectable impact on IFNB1 mRNA accumulation in response to infection with the RNA virus vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), this suggested that rRNA biogenesis selectively influenced IFNB1 induction in response to viruses like HCMV with dsDNA genomes (Figure 4F) (Yanai et al., 2009).
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing IFNB1 response to HCMV versus VSV infection.

claim: The regulation of IFNB1 production by ribosome biogenesis in HCMV infected cells might not require viral gene expression and instead reflect cell intrinsic responses to dsDNA.
source: Moreover, it raised the possibility that the regulation of IFNB1 production by ribosome biogenesis in HCMV infected cells might not require viral gene expression and instead reflect cell intrinsic responses to dsDNA, a pathogen-associated molecule that engages host pattern recognition receptors.
evidence: Speculation based on UV-inactivated HCMV experiments and dsDNA transfection results.

claim: Viral gene expression is not required to induce rRNA accumulation in response to HCMV.
source: Figure 5A shows that UV-inactivated HCMV stimulated 45S rRNA accumulation, which suggested that viral gene expression was not required to induce rRNA accumulation and is consistent with rRNA accumulation being triggered in response to either a virion protein component or a pathogen- associated molecular pattern like a nucleic acid.
evidence: Inference drawn from UV-inactivated HCMV experiment showing 45S rRNA accumulation.

claim: rRNA accumulation is triggered in response to either a virion protein component or a pathogen-associated molecular pattern like a nucleic acid.
source: Figure 5A shows that UV-inactivated HCMV stimulated 45S rRNA accumulation, which suggested that viral gene expression was not required to induce rRNA accumulation and is consistent with rRNA accumulation being triggered in response to either a virion protein component or a pathogen- associated molecular pattern like a nucleic acid.
evidence: Speculation based on UV-inactivated HCMV and dsDNA transfection experiments.

claim: IFNB1 mRNA induction by dsDNA in uninfected primary human fibroblasts is regulated by RNAPI transcription factors.
source: This demonstrates that IFNB1 mRNA induction by dsDNA in uninfected primary human fibroblasts is regulated by RNAPI transcription factors.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing reduced IFNB1 induction upon TIF-IA and UBF depletion in dsDNA-transfected cells.

claim: Mounting an effective cell intrinsic immune response induced by dsDNA-sensing is reliant on RNAPI transcription factors.
source: This suggests that mounting an effective cell intrinsic immune response induced by dsDNA-sensing is reliant on RNAPI transcription factors and consistent with a role for RNAPI activity in this process.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RNA-seq data showing reduced induction of dsDNA-responsive genes upon TIF-IA or UBF depletion.

claim: There is a fundamental connection between rRNA and ribosome biogenesis and innate immune responses in uninfected primary fibroblasts.
source: Moreover, it establishes a fundamental connection between rRNA and ribosome biogenesis and innate immune responses in uninfected primary fibroblasts.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing effects of ribosome biogenesis inhibition on innate immune responses.

claim: Interfering with RNAPI transcription decreases expression of genes involved in cell division, many of which are regulated by NF-Y or the DREAM complex.
source: Genome-wide transcriptome analysis revealed that interfering with rRNA accumulation decreased expression of genes involved in cell division, many of which were regulated by NF-Y or the DREAM complex.
evidence: Summary of RNA-seq and gene ontology analysis results.

claim: Depleting the RNAPI specific transcription factor TIF-IA impaired IFNB1 mRNA accumulation in response to HCMV or dsDNA.
source: Significantly, depleting the RNAPI specific transcription factor TIF-IA impaired IFNB1 mRNA accumulation in response to HCMV or dsDNA.
evidence: Summary of RT-qPCR results from HCMV infection and dsDNA transfection experiments.

claim: Preventing rRNA accumulation dampens cellular responses to dsDNA in part by regulating levels of the DNA sensor HMGB2.
source: Thus, preventing rRNA accumulation dampens cellular responses to dsDNA in part by regulating levels of the DNA sensor HMGB2 (Figure 7F).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing reduced HMGB2 levels and impaired IFNB1 induction.

claim: rRNA biogenesis triggers an HMGB2-dsDNA sensing pathway.
source: Moreover, it suggests that rRNA biogenesis triggers an HMGB2-dsDNA sensing pathway and reveals a surprising role for rRNA accumulation and/or nucleolar activity in cell intrinsic innate immunity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments linking ribosome biogenesis to HMGB2 levels and dsDNA sensing.

claim: rRNA accumulation and/or nucleolar activity play a role in cell intrinsic innate immunity.
source: Moreover, it suggests that rRNA biogenesis triggers an HMGB2-dsDNA sensing pathway and reveals a surprising role for rRNA accumulation and/or nucleolar activity in cell intrinsic innate immunity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing effects of ribosome biogenesis inhibition on innate immune responses.

claim: Inhibiting ribosome biogenesis triggers nucleolar stress, which stabilizes p53 and likely accounts for p53-dependent repression of HMGB2 expression.
source: Inhibiting ribosome biogenesis triggers nucleolar stress, which is known to stabilize p53 (Boulon et al., 2010; Chakraborty et al., 2011; Golomb et al., 2014; Deisenroth et al., 2016) and likely accounts for our observed p53-dependent repression of HMGB2 expression.
evidence: Inference based on established knowledge of nucleolar stress and experimental observation of p53-dependent HMGB2 repression.

claim: HMGB2 levels can be directly tuned to nucleolar stress and dampened accordingly to limit IFNB1 transcription in response to dsDNA sensing.
source: This allows HMGB2 levels to be directly tuned to nucleolar stress and dampened accordingly to limit IFNB1 transcription in response to dsDNA sensing (Figure 7F).
evidence: Inference drawn from the connection between nucleolar stress, p53 stabilization, HMGB2 repression, and IFNB1 induction.

claim: HMGB2 is selectively required for sensing dsDNA, as opposed to RNA, upstream of STING in human cells.
source: That HMGB2-depletion did not detectably impair IFNB1 induction by the RNA virus VSV or cGAMP suggests that HMGB2 is selectively required for sensing dsDNA, as opposed to RNA, upstream of STING in human cells.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing effects of HMGB2 depletion on IFNB1 induction by HCMV, VSV, and cGAMP.

claim: HMGB2 plays a critical role in the induction of IFNB1 by HCMV.
source: Taken together, these results establish a critical role for HMGB2, whose levels decrease in response to TIF-IA-depletion, in the induction of IFNB1 by HCMV.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from HMGB2 depletion experiments showing reduced IFNB1 induction in response to HCMV.

claim: Reducing ribosome biogenesis unexpectedly stimulated HCMV reproduction.
source: Here, we show that while interfering with ribosome biogenesis suppressed ongoing protein synthesis in uninfected primary fibroblasts, it did not detectably impact protein synthesis in HCMV-infected cells. By contrast, reducing ribosome biogenesis unexpectedly stimulated HCMV reproduction.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from virus replication assays.

claim: rRNA accumulation, ribosome biogenesis and DNA sensing can be integrated to coordinate IFNB1 production.
source: Our results show that rRNA accumulation, ribosome biogenesis and DNA sensing can be integrated to coordinate IFNB1 production.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments linking these processes.

claim: RNAP III transcribes cytoplasmic dsDNA into a RIG-I RNA substrate.
source: While RNAP III, which transcribes nuclear genes encoding 5S rRNA and tRNAs, reportedly transcribes cytoplasmic dsDNA into a RIG-I RNA substrate (Chiu et al., 2009), nucleolar or ribosome biogenesis functions of the enzymes were not implicated previously.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Formation of a multipartite complex including STING and S6K is needed to activate IRF3 in response to DNA sensing.
source: Formation of a multipartite complex including STING and S6K is needed to activate IRF3 in response to DNA sensing (Wang et al., 2016)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A ribosomal protein deficiency resulting in Diamond-Blackfan Anemia (DBA) impairs rRNA processing and ribosome biogenesis, resulting in activation of innate immune signaling.
source: A ribosomal protein deficiency resulting in Diamond-Blackfan Anemia (DBA) impairs rRNA processing and ribosome biogenesis, resulting in activation of innate immune signaling (Danilova et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Poliovirus protease 3C(pro) cleaves UBF, which inhibits pol I transcription.
source: The enigmatic cleavage of UBF by poliovirus protease 3C(pro), which inhibits pol I transcription (Banerjee et al., 2005), can now be considered a strategy to limit IFNB1 production.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature and inference about viral strategy.

claim: Antagonizing RNAPI ameliorates experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis in animal models.
source: In addition, antagonizing RNAPI ameliorates experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis in animal models and is associated with a benign course of multiple sclerosis (Achiron et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Proliferative diseases like cancer are associated with hyperactivated rRNA synthesis and ribosome biogenesis.
source: For example, proliferative diseases like cancer are associated with hyperactivated rRNA synthesis and ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: Many tumors have impaired nucleic acid sensing and/or IFN pathways.
source: This could in part account for why many tumors have impaired nucleic acid sensing and/or IFN pathways (Critchley-Thorne et al., 2009; Vanpouille-Box et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature and speculation about mechanism.

claim: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) is characterized by expression of a truncated form of Lamin A called progerin, nucleolar expansion, enhanced ribosome biogenesis, and elevated interferon production.
source: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) is a premature aging disease characterized by expression of a truncated form of Lamin A called progerin, nucleolar expansion, enhanced ribosome biogenesis, and elevated interferon production (Buchwalter and Hetzer, 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: HGPS may be considered an interferonopathy precipitated by pathogenic enhancement of ribosome production.
source: The correlation between ribosome biogenesis and ISG product accumulation raises the possibility that HGPS may be considered an interferonopathy precipitated by pathogenic enhancement of ribosome production.
evidence: Speculation based on correlation between ribosome biogenesis and interferon production.

claim: Patients with Shwachman-Bodian-Diamond Syndrome (SBDS) experience elevated rates of infectious complications.
source: Patients with Shwachman-Bodian-Diamond Syndrome (SBDS), an inherited ribosomopathy characterized by pancreatic, bone marrow, and immune dysfunction (Giri et al., 2015), experience elevated rates of infectious complications, such as those involving Pneumococcus, Staphylococcus, and Parvovirus B19 (Grinspan and Pikora, 2005; Miniero et al., 1996).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Poor innate immune responses, including reduced IFN production, resulting from decreased ribosome biogenesis may contribute to infectious complications in SBDS patients.
source: Poor innate immune responses, including reduced IFN production, resulting from decreased ribosome biogenesis may be a contributing factor.
evidence: Speculation based on findings linking ribosome biogenesis to IFN production.

claim: Increases in rDNA instability caused by nucleolar dysfunction could trigger a DDR, which reportedly can activate cGAS to stimulate increased interferon production.
source: Increases in rDNA instability caused by nucleolar dysfunction could trigger a DDR, which reportedly can activate cGAS to stimulate increased interferon production (Kobayashi, 2008).
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Impairing rRNA accumulation by dampening rRNA synthesis can activate DDR pathways.
source: However, impairing rRNA accumulation by dampening rRNA synthesis also reportedly can activate DDR pathways (Calo et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Failsafe pathways likely detect cytoplasmic dsDNA resulting from rDNA transcription activation, much like cGAS detects cytoplasmic dsDNA during senescence.
source: Nevertheless, failsafe pathways likely detect cytoplasmic dsDNA resulting from rDNA transcription activation, much like cGAS detects cytoplasmic dsDNA during senescence.
evidence: Speculation based on analogy to known cGAS function in senescence.

claim: Activation of dsDNA sensing pathways by ribosome biogenesis might contribute to the reported associations between ribosome biogenesis, lifespan and aging.
source: Activation of dsDNA sensing pathways by ribosome biogenesis might contribute to the reported associations between ribosome biogenesis, lifespan and aging (Sharifi and Bierhoff, 2018; Tiku and Antebi, 2018).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to prior literature on ribosome biogenesis and aging.

claim: By activating cytoplasmic dsDNA-sensing, rDNA instability resulting from elevated ribosome biogenesis observed in HGPS could accelerate senescence and thereby drive the progression and severity of premature aging.
source: For example, by activating cytoplasmic dsDNA-sensing, rDNA instability resulting from elevated ribosome biogenesis observed in HGPS could accelerate senescence and thereby drive the progression and severity of premature aging.
evidence: Speculation about mechanism in HGPS based on findings linking ribosome biogenesis to dsDNA sensing.

claim: The underlying mechanism(s) for why infected compared to uninfected cell protein synthesis is insensitive to interfering with ribosome biogenesis are potentially multifaceted and complex.
source: Although polysome levels and protein synthesis were not detectably altered by TIF-IA-depletion in HCMV-infected fibroblasts, precisely why infected compared to uninfected cell protein synthesis was insensitive to interfering with ribosome biogenesis remains unknown. The underlying mechanism(s) are potentially multifaceted and complex perhaps involving virus-induced increases in cellular translation factors that allow more efficient use of existing ribosomes (McKinney et al., 2012; McKinney et al., 2014), differences among ribosome populations, cis-acting elements (Mizrahi et al., 2018) in host and viral mRNAs being translated, specific virus-encoded polypeptides, and/or the differential complexity of mRNA populations in uninfected compared to HCMV-infected cells.
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Sustained protein synthesis despite reduced nucleolar volume and rRNA synthesis has been observed in germline stem cell differentiation in Drosophila.
source: Notably, sustained protein synthesis despite reduced nucleolar volume and rRNA synthesis has been observed in germline stem cell differentiation in Drosophila (Neumüller et al., 2008; Sanchez et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature in Drosophila.

claim: rRNA synthesis is not required for growth factor-mediated hypertrophy of human primary myotubes.
source: Likewise, rRNA synthesis is not required for growth factor-mediated hypertrophy of human primary myotubes (Crossland et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: rRNA and ribosome biogenesis can be uncoupled from protein synthesis in invertebrates and in primary human cells.
source: Thus, rRNA and ribosome biogenesis can be uncoupled from protein synthesis in invertebrates and in primary human cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from cited examples in Drosophila and human myotubes.

claim: 45S pre-rRNA synthesis was stimulated in response to HCMV infection at 30 hr post-infection.
source: Earlier studies (Tanaka et al., 1975) indicated that 45S pre-rRNA synthesis was stimulated in response to HCMV infection at 30 hr post-infection (hpi).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: HCMV is a large DNA virus that replicates in the nucleus.
source: HCMV is a large DNA virus that replicates in the nucleus and although wide-spread and commonly asymptomatic, infection results in life-threatening disease among the immunocompromised and remains a major source of congenital morbidity and mortality among newborns (Boeckh and Geballe, 2011; Britt, 2008; Cannon et al., 2010; Ljungman et al., 2010; Manicklal et al., 2013; Razonable et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge with citations to prior literature.

claim: HCMV infection results in life-threatening disease among the immunocompromised.
source: HCMV is a large DNA virus that replicates in the nucleus and although wide-spread and commonly asymptomatic, infection results in life-threatening disease among the immunocompromised and remains a major source of congenital morbidity and mortality among newborns (Boeckh and Geballe, 2011; Britt, 2008; Cannon et al., 2010; Ljungman et al., 2010; Manicklal et al., 2013; Razonable et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HCMV remains a major source of congenital morbidity and mortality among newborns.
source: HCMV is a large DNA virus that replicates in the nucleus and although wide-spread and commonly asymptomatic, infection results in life-threatening disease among the immunocompromised and remains a major source of congenital morbidity and mortality among newborns (Boeckh and Geballe, 2011; Britt, 2008; Cannon et al., 2010; Ljungman et al., 2010; Manicklal et al., 2013; Razonable et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HCMV relies upon multiple independent mechanisms to mitigate cellular antiviral immune responses without globally impairing translation of host mRNAs.
source: To mitigate cellular antiviral immune responses without globally impairing translation of host mRNAs, HCMV relies upon multiple independent mechanisms (Biolatti et al., 2018; Li et al., 2013; Paulus and Nevels, 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One mechanism HCMV uses involves a virus-directed increase in the abundance of host translation factors.
source: One of these involves a virus-directed increase in the abundance of host translation factors, suggesting a viral mechanism to facilitate simultaneous synthesis of host and viral proteins (Tirosh et al., 2015; McKinney et al., 2014; Perez et al., 2011; Walsh et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HCMV-induced increases in host translational machinery have been shown to be required for efficient viral replication.
source: Indeed, HCMV-induced increases in host translational machinery have been shown to be required for efficient viral replication (McKinney et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.
